_: THE ONE LIST BOTH PLANES ARE TESTED AGAINST (#1173, #1119, ADR 0099 §2).
`display_condition` is parsed and evaluated in TWO LANGUAGES, and that is not a
choice anybody made. The authority is Go: facet.SplitFieldTerm, the same
function the search `filter=field:...` predicate uses, reused verbatim so that a
condition and a filter cannot disagree about what a term means. THE BROWSER
CANNOT CALL IT. So there are two implementations of one grammar:
app/internal/metadata/display_condition.go   (server; delegates to
facet.SplitFieldTerm)
web/src/lib/displayCondition.ts               (client; reimplements the same
five properties)
Two implementations of one rule drift. This file is what stops them: both suites
READ IT rather than carrying their own copy of the case list, so a change that
moves one plane fails on the other plane's test rather than being noticed months
later by an operator whose field will not appear.
Read by app/internal/metadata/display_condition_parity_test.go and
web/src/lib/displayCondition.test.ts. If you add a case here, both pick it up.
THE FIVE PROPERTIES THE `parse` SECTION PINS, none of them guessable:
1. split on the FIRST character from `=~<>`
2. operators matched LONGEST FIRST, so `>=` is never `>` then `=value`
3. later operator characters stay IN the value
4. the CODE is lowercased and trimmed
5. the parsed VALUE is trimmed
AND THE ONE THE `evaluate` SECTION PINS: nothing ever trims or case-folds the
STORED value. That asymmetry with (5) is the discriminator case below, and it is
the thing an operator will actually hit.

parse.why: the ordinary term
property 4 and 5 together: the CODE is trimmed AND lowercased, the VALUE is trimmed. The stored value it will be compared against is not touched at all.
`~` parses like any other operator, and the literal keeps its case here; case-insensitivity is a property of the MATCH, not of the parse
property 1 and 3: split on the FIRST `=`, and the second one stays in the value
property 3 again with a different operator character: `~` inside an `=` value is part of the value
property 1 with the operators the other way round: `~` comes first, so `=` is in the value
property 2: LONGEST FIRST. `>=` is one operator, not `>` followed by a value beginning `=`. It parses fine and is refused separately by the display-condition matrix, which is a different rule.
the other bound, same reasoning
property 2 from the other side: `=>` is NOT an operator. The split takes `=`, and `>x` is the value.

⛔ AN EMBEDDED NEWLINE SURVIVES, AND THIS IS ONE TERM. `TrimSpace` strips only the ENDS of the parsed value, `validFieldCode` constrains only the code, and the storage CHECK asks only for a non-empty string. So a value may legitimately contain a newline, which is why the admin editor maps one CONTROL to one ARRAY ELEMENT and uses no delimiter at all: a line-delimited editor would load this as two terms and save the second one back with no operator.
the ENDS are still trimmed around an internal newline, so the leading and trailing spaces go and the newline stays
a BLANK LINE inside the value is preserved too; nothing collapses runs of whitespace in the middle
a newline BEFORE the operator is part of the CODE, which no field code may contain, so this is malformed. The asymmetry with the cases above is the point: the value is permissive, the code is not.
MALFORMED: no operator at all, so there is nothing to split on
MALFORMED: an EMPTY parsed value. `code=` says nothing, and guessing that it means the empty string would silently hide every field whose controller is unset.
MALFORMED: a whitespace-only value trims to empty, which is the same nothing
MALFORMED: an empty code. There is no field to name.
MALFORMED: a code carrying a character no field code may hold. Field codes are [a-z0-9_-]; the parser lowercases first, so case is not what fails here, the space is.

MALFORMED: a `field:` PREFIX is not stored and is not accepted. The colon is not a legal code character, so a caller pasting a search token in gets a refusal rather than a term naming a field called `field:work_type`.
a code may hold digits, an underscore and a hyphen, and an uppercase one is folded rather than refused

evaluate.why: `=` IS CASE-SENSITIVE. This is not a near miss to be forgiven; the same operator is case-sensitive in the search predicate, and a condition that disagreed with the filter would be a second grammar.

⚠️ THE DISCRIMINATOR. The condition literal is TRIMMED by the parser and the STORED value is not. So `work_type= Commission ` parses to the literal `Commission`, and a stored value of ` Commission ` is six characters longer and does NOT match. An evaluator that trimmed the stored value would pass this and would disagree with `=` everywhere else in the product.
the same stored value DOES match a literal that survives trimming to the same thing, which is what makes the case above about the STORED side rather than about whitespace in general
a readable controller holding NOTHING is a REAL FALSE. Absence is an answer, and treating it as unknown produces an evaluator that never hides anything.
`~` is a CASE-INSENSITIVE SUBSTRING match, so the literal's case is irrelevant on both sides

controller.text: Please treat as URGENT before Friday

evaluate.why: `~` still has to be a substring; a shared prefix is not a match
`~` against an empty stored value. The empty string is a substring of everything, but nothing is a substring of the empty string, so this is FALSE rather than a surprise TRUE.
a term whose value carries a newline evaluates like any other: `~` still matches it as a case-insensitive substring of the stored value

controller.text:
PREFIX line one
line two SUFFIX

evaluate.why: and it does NOT match a stored value that has a space where the newline is, so the newline is really part of the comparison rather than incidental whitespace
a `select` compares the stored SLUG, because ADR 0012 keeps only the slug on the record
and it does not match the label an operator might have typed instead
a `tree` value is ONE leaf slug in value_text, not a path, so it compares exactly like a select
MEMBERSHIP: on a multi_select `=` asks whether the term is one of the stored values, not whether it is all of them
membership still misses when the term is not in the set
membership is case-sensitive too, for `=`'s reason
an empty option set is a readable controller with no value, which is a REAL FALSE

condition.why: N=0. No condition means always shown, and no term is examined.
N=1 FALSE arm. Both arms are required: an evaluator that only ever shows passes every true-arm test.
N>=2 case 1 — A true, B true -> SHOWN
N>=2 case 2 — A true, B false -> HIDDEN
N>=2 case 3 — A false, B true -> HIDDEN. The conjunction is order-independent.

⛔ N>=2 case 4 — A FALSE, B's DEFINITION MISSING -> SHOWN. This is the case a naive 'unknown counts as true inside the AND' gets wrong: `false AND true` would still HIDE. Once any term is unevaluable the condition has NO VERDICT and the remaining terms are not consulted.
⛔ N>=2 case 5 — A FALSE, B UNREADABLE -> SHOWN, for the same reason. `readable` is a server-derived fact and never an inference from whether a value arrived.
N>=2 case 6 — A READABLE BUT UNSET, B true -> HIDDEN. The mirror trap: readable absence is a REAL FALSE, not unknown.
an UNPARSEABLE term makes the whole condition unevaluable, even when a sibling term is plainly false

an operator the controller's TYPE does not accept is unevaluable rather than false. Configuration refuses this pairing, so reaching it means the definition changed under a stored condition, which is later drift and fails open.
DUPLICATE IDENTICAL TERMS are legal and evaluate as one
two MEMBERSHIP terms on one multi_select can both be true, which is why they are legal configuration where two `=` on a single-valued controller are not
and they conjoin properly: holding one of the two is not enough
N=3 with one unreadable among two TRUE terms: still SHOWN, because unevaluable is unevaluable regardless of what the others say
